content.title: Solving Linear and Compound Inequalities
content.overview: This lesson focuses on how to solve one-variable linear inequalities and compound inequalities connected by "and" or "or." Mastering these skills is the foundation for solving complex constraint problems in the SAT Math section.
learning_objectives: Master the basic steps for solving one-variable linear inequalities.
Understand the change in inequality direction when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number.
Learn to solve compound inequalities containing "and" and "or."
Be able to represent inequality solution sets using number lines or intervals.

sections.title: Basic Properties of Linear Inequalities
sections.content: The process of solving a one-variable linear inequality is very similar to solving an equation, with the goal of isolating the variable. Basic properties include: 1. Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides does not change the direction of the inequality. 2. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive number does not change the direction of the inequality. 3. Key Rule: When multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number, you must flip the direction of the inequality sign (e.g., from < to >).

sections.title: Compound Inequalities: 'AND' and 'OR'
sections.content: Compound inequalities consist of two simple inequalities. 1. 'AND' Compound Inequalities: Require the variable to satisfy both conditions simultaneously; the solution set is the intersection (overlap) of the two solutions. It is often written in the form a < x < b. 2. 'OR' Compound Inequalities: The variable only needs to satisfy at least one of the conditions; the solution set is the union (combination) of the two solutions.

sections.title: Representing Solution Sets
sections.content:
Solutions to inequalities are typically represented as intervals or marked on a number line. On a number line, an open circle indicates that the endpoint is not included (< or >), while a solid dot indicates that the endpoint is included (≤ or ≥). For compound inequalities, an intersection appears as a line segment between two points, while a union usually appears as rays extending in opposite directions.

![Number Line Representation of Inequality x > -2](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/fa29b9ec-a7be-4300-a7cb-cb011d7b0a33-1786502038538-919.webp)

worked_examples.question: Solve the inequality: -3x + 7 ≤ 22
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Subtract 7 from both sides to get -3x ≤ 15. Step 2: Divide both sides by -3. Note that because you are dividing by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign. The result is x ≥ -5.

worked_examples.question: Solve the compound inequality: 2x - 5 > 1 AND 3x + 2 < 17
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Solve the first inequality 2x > 6, which gives x > 3. Step 2: Solve the second inequality 3x < 15, which gives x < 5. Step 3: Take the intersection; the solution set is 3 < x < 5.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Confusing the logical meanings of "AND" (intersection) and "OR" (union).
Incorrectly using open and solid circles on the number line.
exam_tips: If the question asks for the minimum or maximum integer value satisfying the inequality, find the exact solution set first, then determine the integer based on the boundary conditions.
When dealing with compound inequalities, if there is no overlap between the two conditions, the system has no solution.
Quick Check: Pick a number from your solution set and plug it into the original inequality to verify if it holds true.
content.recap: The core of solving linear inequalities lies in handling sign flips during negative multiplication or division. Compound inequalities require determining whether the final solution set is an intersection or a union based on the logical connectors (AND/OR).

knowledge_claims.content: When multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality sign must be flipped.
Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides of an inequality keeps the direction of the inequality sign unchanged.
The solution set of an 'AND' compound inequality is the intersection of the solutions of the two individual inequalities.
The solution set of an 'OR' compound inequality is the union of the solutions of the two individual inequalities.
On a number line, an open circle indicates that the endpoint is not included in the solution set (corresponding to < or >).
On a number line, a solid dot indicates that the endpoint is included in the solution set (corresponding to ≤ or ≥).
When solving a continuous inequality of the form a < bx + c < d, the same algebraic operations can be performed on all three parts simultaneously to isolate x.
It is a mistake to believe that dividing both sides of an inequality by a positive number also requires flipping the inequality sign.
If the two conditions of an 'AND' compound inequality have no overlapping region, then the compound inequality has no solution.
The correctness of a solution can be verified by selecting a test value from the calculated solution set and substituting it into the original inequality.
